This is an 18-month-old male with acute, non-traumatic hemarthrosis of the right knee — a classic presenting sign of a severe congenital coagulopathy. The isolated prolongation of ACT (aPTT-equivalent) with preserved extrinsic (PT) and common pathway (thrombin time) function localizes the defect to the intrinsic pathway — specifically factors VIII, IX, XI, or XII. Among these, only FVIII and FIX deficiencies cause spontaneous hemarthrosis in early childhood; FXI deficiency typically presents later and with milder, trauma-triggered bleeding; FXII deficiency is asymptomatic. The X-linked recessive family history — maternal uncle with “similar problems” — is highly specific for hemophilia A or B. - No alternative explanation (e.g., trauma, malignancy, autoimmune disease) identified on history or exam

- Factor IX activity level — needed to definitively exclude hemophilia B  
- von Willebrand factor antigen and activity — though less likely given isolated aPTT prolongation and hemarthrosis (vWD type 3 could mimic, but is autosomal recessive and rarer; family history points to X-linked)  
- Genetic testing (F8 gene sequencing) — confirmatory but not urgent for initial diagnosis
